newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - limited RPI impact from BoE independence.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - limited RPI impact from BoE independence.

text.p: The Bank of England's newly-won independence to set interest rates has been welcomed by economists as an effective weapon to fight long-term inflation, but most forecasters said they had yet to alter their end-1997 predictions, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday.

Twenty of the 22 contributors to the survey, conducted on Wednesday, said they saw operational independence for the central bank to set interest rates would be "effective" in curbing inflation. One said the move would be "very effective", while one said it would make no difference.

Despite the enthusiasm for the move, 17 said they had left their end-year predictions for retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments (RPIX) unchanged, while five said they had revised down their figures.

After Labour's victory in Britain's May 1 general election, the new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown surprised the financial markets by giving the Bank of England (BoE) the operational leeway to set interest rates.
With the advice of a monetary committee, the BoE will be allowed to adjust rates in order to meet inflation targets for RPIX -- currently 2.5 percent -- set by the Treasury.

In its quarterly inflation report released on Tuesday, the Bank of England said market moves after its new freedom was announced showed inflation expectations over the long-term -- five to 10 years down the line -- had dropped by half a percent.

Previously, former Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Eddie George, Governor of BoE used to meet once every four weeks to discuss inflation prospects and the need to adjust interest rates.
Many of the economists surveyed said that although they thought the new system would be effective, it was not replacing a bad system.
"The previous arrangement was good and satisfactory. The latest development is just an incremental improvement," said Phillip Shaw, UK economist at Union Plc.
Many economists said they were waiting until Brown makes his first budget before making a change to their inflation outlook, as fiscal prudence was as important as stringent monetary policy.
"The BoE will try to be responsible, but it is crucial to see what happens in the mini-budget," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale in London.

Economists said the BoE inflation report sent a coded message to Brown that taxes needed to rise. The report admitted that higher interest rates would dampen domestic demand but would also, if they pushed the pound higher, widen the gap between struggling manufacturers and buoyant retailers.

"This is a clearly coded message for the Chancellor," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel. "They are saying as explicitly as they can that if the government puts taxes up they will not raise rates too far."
Expectations are for Brown to present a budget in June. April RPIX, due on Thursday, is expected to rise 2.6 percent year-on-year from 2.7 percent in March.

Some said the risks of leaving the Bank to work with an exact inflation target may provoke a tendency to err on the side of caution and could in turn wreak havoc on employment levels and economic growth.
"I would rather see a target range of two to three percent," said James Shugg, economist at Westpac. "With a target range there is less tendency to over-compensate."
James McKay, UK economist at Paine Webber, said he expected BoE independence to be very effective in curbing inflation.

"It depoliticises monetary policy. If the government chooses to run an expansionary fiscal policy, the central bank can offset with tighter monetary policy. Also the BoE is not bound by the political cycle," he said.

Nick Stamenkovic, UK economist at DKB International, said he believed BoE independence would make no difference to long-term inflation. There was no evidence to suggest that more independence had a beneficial influence on inflation, he said.
Five contributors said they had revised down their forecasts for RPIX since the election.
"But only because of our changed outlook for sterling exchange rates," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS, who believes the British currency will stay firm.
Sterling has risen by more than 20 percent versus the mark since last August.
The effects of sterling strength can be seen in the latest producer output prices, which rose by 0.8 percent year-on-year in April compared with a one-percent rise in March.

The mean of the 22 forecasts for RPIX at end-1997 was 2.5 percent. This compares with an average 2.7 percent figure forecast in the Reuters survey of forecasts for the British economy conducted in April.
